preamble: Depharyngealization of the voiced pharyngeal [ʕ] (Semitic ʿayin) to the glottal stop [ʔ] moves the constriction from the pharynx down to the glottis. It is a recurrent outcome in Semitic: Standard Israeli Hebrew merged ע with א as /ʔ/ (or zero), Amharic lost its pharyngeals by the end of the medieval period so that the ʿayin series of the Ge'ez script is now read [ʔ], and the Urmia dialect of Assyrian Neo-Aramaic turned Aramaic ʿayin into [ʔ] (ʿammā > Urmia [ʔam.mɑː] 'people'), while Standard Assyrian keeps [ʕ]. Persian, which has no pharyngeals, substitutes [ʔ] for ʿayin in its many Arabic loanwords.

examples.note: Biblical ʕ and ʔ generally merged into Israeli /ʔ/ or became silent; the distinction is maintained in the speech of older Sephardim.
Pre-17th-century Amharic still distinguished /ʔ/ and /ʕ/; phonological change merged them, so the ʿayin (ዐ) and ʾalef (አ) series of the script both represent [ʔ].
Written with the ʿayin letter ዐ but pronounced with the glottal stop, which is optional word-initially.
Urmia replaces ʿayin with the glottal stop; Classical Syriac ܥܡܐ [ʕammɑ] and Standard Assyrian [ʕam.mɑː] keep [ʕ].
Classical Syriac ܥܝܢܐ [ʕajnɑ] and Standard Assyrian [ʕaj.nɑː] keep [ʕ]; Nineveh Plains has [ʔeːnɑː], with the same glottal onset.
Loanword adaptation: Persian has no pharyngeals, so ع is pronounced [ʔ], merging with ء.
Medial ʿayin is realised as a glottal stop.
